utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is K54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the protective measures for this witness are what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, he has face protection and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we shall go into closed session while --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The courtroom. Sorry. Just one moment. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, before the witness enters, Defence submitted a motion seeking to exclude this witness completely and the Bench refused our application. Before the witness enters, defence submitted a motion seeking to exclude this witness completely and the Bench refused our application. Before the witness enters, wanted to put another motion forth by which we would ask that certain portions of his testimony be excluded. We saw that he would be a combination of 92 ter and a live witness. We asked that his statement on three incidents pertaining to 1999 be excluded; they were not made part of the indictment, and I may offer additional arguments. These are the incidents pertaining to the 28th of February, 1999, in Ljubizda Has and then another one in mid-March in Jeskovo and then the 25th of March in the village of in Trnje. What is particularly of our concern is the Trnje incident, which was not stipulated, neither in the indictment nor in the pre-trial brief and it wasn't to be found in the information according to the Rule 65 ter. When it comes to this latest incident in the village of Trnje on the 25th of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean, Mr. Bakrac, that it's not in 65 ter. You must have received the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we received the witness's statement in September or somewhat later. This witness-- or rather, the material pertaining to him was disclosed later, but in the 65 ter summary, which is also another argument I wanted to use, it is stated that he is to testify on the incident that took place on the 25th of March south to the village of Mamusa in the municipality of Prizren. At the time when the 65 ter summary was compiled and significantly prior to the indictment in 2003, almost four years ago, and three years before the amendments to the indictment, this statement went to the location and showed the villages mentioned in his statement to the investigators. On that occasion he identified the village of Trnje and the OTP has had that information for three years. We were told he was to testify on the village south of Mamusa in the municipality of Prizren. The village of Trnje is to the east of Mamusa. And I can go back to the disclosure list. The witness is -- on the 16th of July, 2002, that is almost five years ago, the witness went there with the OTP investigators and at page 1 of supplemental information dated the 16th of July and then revised in page 5, paragraph 4 he mentions Suva Reka and Trnje. First of all, the village of Trnje and the incident pertaining to that village is not in the indictment and it is not in the pre-trial brief, although since 2002 that incident was identified particularly by this witness and linked to the village of Trnje. In the 65 ter summary we received concerning another incident that may appear similar, we were told that that incident will be addressed by the witness concerning a village south, which is to the south of Mamusa and Trnje is to the east. Another thing we wanted to stress because of the need for a fair trial which far exceeds the probative value which witness has to offer, if we go to the transcript from a previous trial, and because of the protective measures and at the end of that testimony the -- Judge Kwon asked him when he went to that location whether he showed to the investigators the exact spot where five female victims had been buried, killed during the incident that I am talking about. The witness said no, but the investigators said that that location was known to them. Since we are still in 2003, and this witness claims that the investigators knew of that location, we received no notification of the victims or any type of notification which would state that the victims pertaining to that incident had been found. Why do I mention the need for a fair trial and that it far exceeds the probative value of this testimony pertaining to this part of it? Well, it would be unfair to the accused to have an incident which could serve to show a pattern of behaviour to be taken as something that had been proven, whereas on the other hand, the OTP, apart from the witness statement, has no list of victims and it was never established who exactly those victims were. And on top of it all, that incident is not corroborated by any other evidence or proof. Therefore, we believe that the testimony of this witness should not include the three aforementioned incidents, the one from Ljubizda Has which is not to be found neither in the indictment nor in the pre-trial brief, then the second incident of Jeskovo and then the third one of Trnje for all the aforementioned reasons. The Trnje incident, as treated in the supplemental information, is stated as Trnje/Suva Reka, but that incident has nothing to do with the incident in Suva Reka dated the 25th of March. These are two separate locations. The village of Trnje is halfway to Prizren when going from Suva Reka and has got nothing to do with the 25th of March Suva Reka incident. That is why I believe it would be unfair to the accused to have this testimony in its entirety for all the reasons I have mentioned. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is the incident in Jeskovo in this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps my learned friend may assist me. I have before me the B/C/S. It's in my version, paragraph 3, page 5, and if I may have a moment, I may be able to provide the paragraph and page reference in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I may assist --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Page 5, the first paragraph, I think, deals with Jeskovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it actually named in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not in the statement, but in the supplemental information, the P number being 2673 dated the 16th of July, 2002, it reads: "Correction or addition, paragraph 6, page 4, Jeskovo." As far as I understand it, in that supplemental information of the 16th of July, 2005, this is where we can find it. It was almost five years ago and four years after the pre-trial brief and the amended indictment. And if I may add something regarding the principle of fair trial. The accused were not put on sufficient notice concerning the specific allegations that have to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the paragraph -- the first incident you referred to was the 28th of March -- sorry, 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the 28th of February, Ljubizda Has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the most drastic example is the third incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the first one, though, is that referred to in the paragraph before Jeskovo? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Trnje follows immediately the incident in Jeskovo and I believe it is the most drastic example concerning the arguments I put forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, several points. First of all, to start with, the last issue we just discussed. The two incidents just shortly before the NATO bombing started, we -- that was already subject to the written filings and we submitted in this regard that they are relevant to paragraph 99 of the indictment, which explicitly charges that, in late February and early March, forces of the FRY and Serbia launched a series of offensives against dozens of predominantly Kosovo Albanian villages and town during the peace negotiations in France. So this is the very period concerned and the evidence is relevant in this regard. Your Honours already decided on many of the arguments Mr. Bakrac repeated now, I think, in your decision of 15th February 2007 on the relevance and admissibility of this witness's evidence. As regards Trnje village, the incident is mentioned in the 65 ter summary. There is a reference in the fourth paragraph to the killing of 15 people, including women and children. It's correct what Mr. Bakrac says, that the reference is to a village south of Mamusa. Now, this was- because at some point it wasn't really clear from the witness's evidence which village it was this killing took place in, and only after he visited the site with the investigator it became clear that it was actually Trnje village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: He confirmed that also in his live evidence in Milosevic, and it is nobody's fault but mine that I didn't change it in the 65 ter summary to say "Trnje." However, the Defence has had the statement and the testimony from Milosevic, everything, since the day we applied to have this witness added to the list, which was late last year, and they were perfectly aware of where this killing occurred. So I don't think this is a valid argument really of lack of notice because it's clear from all the material that was given to them for the witness that it was, indeed, in the village of Trnje. And at the end of the day, the substance which is set out in the 65 ter summary; namely, what really happened, who was killed, is exactly the same as appears in his evidence. So it's really just the concrete location where there may have been some unclarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date of the application to add this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It was in November, I think. I would have to check the exact date. No, sorry, it was 8 September 2006, actually. I would also like to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would also like to address the point raised about whether or not the human remains of the victims of the killing in Trnje were actually exhumed and there is any information in the office that we haven't disclosed. The witness told me in the proofing this time again that an investigator told him that we knew more about that. I haven't been able to see any information on that, and from my internal investigations, there was no exhumation, so we don't have the names of the victims. As far as I could find out, in 2002, when all these events and the two witnesses who were able to talk about these events came to the knowledge of the OTP, there wasn't any possibility to do further exhumations in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He says in his evidence that he marked a spot where certain bodies were buried. Is that the site that we're talking about, where five people were buried?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And no one's made any effort to locate it, is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that, to my knowledge, there hasn't been any possibility given for this case to do further investigations in this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean nobody's tried to find this site -- this location, in spite of what the witness has said? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm telling you is because it was at the very late stage in the Milosevic case and the Kosovo investigations were at the advanced stage, there wasn't any exhumation done. The focus was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's not my question. Are you saying you haven't even found the location? It was marked but -- he said he marked it in a particular way. Has no one tried to find it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, according to the witness an investigator went there and had a look at the site, but this investigator is no longer here. I'm trying -- I tried to verify it, but from the investigation section, as it is today, I couldn't retrieve any positive information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in this whole matter of it, the thing I have greatest difficulty with is why Trnje is not in the indictment. I asked the question in the Milosevic trial -- at least when I read my way into that trial, it was a striking feature of this incident that it wasn't in his indictment either. And it's -- coincides with the whole theme of your case, which is as of the NATO bombing there is this ethnic cleansing campaign. So what -- why was this -- nothing done after the Milosevic trial to put this particular incident into the indictment? Because if it's not, it's an incident that on the face of it bears direct comparison with the various ones which are specified and you would be asking us to make very specific findings about it to the prejudice of the accused without ever indicting them for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with all due respect to the victims of this incident, it is a comparatively small and minor killing, if one can say that about any killing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the 50 to 60 who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, I mean we have only -- in regard to this incident, we have two witnesses who testified about that, and they testified about having seen a number of people being killed during the operation in the village, but we don't have any evidence from any witnesses there, from any victims there, and we don't have the identification of the people killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your 65 ter summary says: "The witness saw soldiers force 15 people, including women and children, out of a home, line them up, and shoot them in a courtyard. He estimates around 50 to 60 civilians were killed in the operation. He was then involved in actually disposing of some of the bodies." And you say that this is minor compared with others in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Indeed it is, Your Honours, because it's already from the larger incidents that we have, as you know, three were excluded from this indictment. So at the time we were preparing this case, we were only looking at streamlining the case and boiling it down but not to extending it, and that was, of course, one of the major thoughts behind that. But also on the basis of the evidence we had available at the time, it was not detailed enough to really present it as a charged crime site, because it would have involved extensive investigations into this matter because, as I said, we had some testimony about persons who took part in the operation, but we were not or are not in possession of much other evidence on these accounts. So we would have had to investigate this extensively. And in light of the multiplicity of murder incidents we had already charged, we didn't find it necessary to charge one more in the indictment. And I just want to underline once more that we're not trying to lead this evidence as a murder count or as proof for the murder. It is, as we submitted in our -- in our written submissions on the admissibility of this evidence, it is evidence that goes to the question whether a certain style of operations was conducted all over Kosovo, whether there was a joint criminal enterprise, and in this regard we still maintain that it does not need to be set out in the indictment as a murder count. One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not specified as a deportation count, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because it's not a deportation incident, actually. It's just another example of how forces conducted so-called anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not leading it as evidence of murder or as proof of a murder. So what are you leading it as evidence of?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We are leading it as evidence of the many allegations in the indictment of how operations were conducted by the army during the relevant period in the relevant municipalities that excessive and discriminate force was used over and again and that included mistreatment and also killing and other things, but it's just to show this kind of behaviour of the forces; also to show that there must have been a joint criminal enterprise which included this way of operating in so-called anti-terrorist operations. We also lead this evidence to show which forces were actually in the area, because although this particular witness can't give you any brigade names or any other things, he can give you the names of many commanding officers and we have the corresponding documents, military documents, which show then who was where when in the area. This is highly relevant to the indictment, as you have always pointed out that we make sure to verify that actually forces that were under the command of these accused were operating in the area. He's also giving that evidence, and there are many other aspects his evidence goes to, as we have argued in the written submissions that you have received on the 12th of February. If I may add one aspect why the Trnje incident wasn't charged in the indictment, I forgot to mention that, as I said, we have two witnesses who can testify to these events, and both of them were witnesses also in the Milosevic case, both of them had quite some problems after testifying in the Milosevic case. And one of them, K82, we had decided not to hear, also had some other problems that made it likely at the time that we would actually never get him here to testify. This witness, who is due to testify today, after Milosevic expressed unwillingness to ever testify again and only late last year, just before we filed the application to add him, suddenly he changed his mind and was willing to come again. So this was another reason we couldn't add Trnje, because these two witnesses who were actually the foundation of this incident were more than unlikely to ever come. We were positively surprised ourselves last year that it worked out that they would actually come. So this was another reason to decide not to add a count to the indictment on this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber will adjourn to consider this. --- Break taken at 9.31 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first two incidents referred to by Mr. Bakrac seem to relate to matters that we have already decided the witness should be permitted to give evidence about. The third one, Trnje, is closely related and offered by the Prosecution as evidence of the general nature of the conduct of particular sections of the VJ and the police. As you all know, we have already decided that this evidence is, in principle -- this evidence of this type and in relation to these areas is in principle admissible. However, we intend to reserve the question of whether to admit the evidence until after we have heard it, and that applies to the evidence in relation to all three locations. If admitted -- and there's a significant chance that that will happen subject, obviously, to developments as we listen carefully to it, but if that evidence is admitted, the decision to admit it is potentially inconsistent with the decision we took in relation to the evidence of K82. We are obviously in an entirely different situation now and we have a much greater knowledge of the circumstances, not only of the events that are being -- that are the subject of this case but also much greater knowledge of how the case is to be or has been presented. We would, therefore, be willing to consider an application, if it were made to us, to reconsider our decision in relation to K82; however, if it was intended to make such an application, it would have to be done more or less instantly. Now, by that, I mean certainly sometime in the course of this week and I would have thought Wednesday was a reasonable deadline. That's a different decision, in fact, from deciding whether to admit the evidence of K54, but as I say, and bearing in mind the apparent inconsistency that would arise, then it would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber to have submissions on the question of whether we should reconsider that decision, should the -- early, should the Prosecution have that in mind. So we will now proceed to hear the evidence of this witness. We need to go into closed session for him to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will refer to you as Witness K54. You know that that's one of the methods being used to protect your identity and thus your security. In addition, your appearance will be distorted on the television screens that display this evidence so that you cannot be recognised from your appearance in court. We have seen a statement that you gave and then an addendum, an addition to that statement, and we have also seen a transcript of your evidence in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. The purpose of having you here today is to enable the counsel involved in the case to ask additional questions to clarify things, to expand the information, and in some instances to challenge your evidence. You will assist us greatly if you can concentrate on the particular question that you're asked and try to restrict your answer to dealing with the point that is raised with you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first person to ask questions will be for the Prosecution, and that will be Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I will show you a piece of paper with some data on it. I would like you to confirm that this is your name and your correct data, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Exhibit P2668 and I would tender this under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a statement to the -- to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in April 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in July 2002 did you give an addendum statement as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came here last week to testify in this trial, did you have the opportunity to have both statements read back to you or did you read it back yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in the process of that, did you point out some small corrections to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In particular, in relation to your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's page 4 of the English version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You are talking about an incident that occurred at Ljubizda Has on the 28th of February, 1999. Your statement says that all combat groups were deployed to this location. Did you make a correction to this statement and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Not all the combat groups were mentioned there but only part of them, that is to say the entire barracks. I mean the entire barracks was involved in this action, and a part, a small part, of the combat groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know which combat groups were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Combat Group 2, it was stationed there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to another incident you deal with in your -- in both of your statements as well as in the transcript, this is the incident at Trnje. And it is not quite clear from the different statements where you actually were when the killing of the 15 civilians occurred and you made some further explanations in this regard in the proofing, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this relates to the statement page 5, the addendum, the first page, and in the transcript it is pages 8307 and 8308.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, can you clarify when you were -- when the sergeant removed the family from the house and the civilians were shot, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I was at this small hill, this little hill, and I was far away from that location, actually, a hundred metres away and I saw clearly what was going on there. I mean I could see this well what was going on, what was being done, and later on I came and saw all of that -- I mean the dead and the killed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: While you were on the hill, what exactly did you see in relation to this incident, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I saw my -- I mean our troops, that combat group of mine where I was, taking civilians out of the house and putting them between the house and a wall and, quite simply, opening bursts of gun-fire at them and killing all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you mention a particular officer who participated in this incident. How did you recognise this officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: He always had this cloth on his head when he went into action instead of a military cap. I recognised him by that. He used that in previous actions and in this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you see him participate in this shooting with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with these corrections and clarifications added to your two statements, do you attest today that what you -- what you testified to in the statement of April and July 2002 is true and correct to the best of your knowledge and that you would testify the same if you were asked all these questions again today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you also testify in the trial against Slobodan Milosevic in 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after you testified, did you receive a copy of the tape that showed your testimony in this trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: What do you mean? What do you mean? Did I receive what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you get a copy of your testimony on tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I asked for that. I asked to be given that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And since then, have you viewed this video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many times have you viewed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came here last week, did you also have the opportunity to have parts of your transcript read back to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, I did have this opportunity of having it read back to me, this testimony of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in regard to your transcript, did you point out one correction you wished to make in relation to a soldier that is mentioned therein with the name Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. In your transcript, that's page 8242, lines 19 to 23, you referred to a soldier named Milosevic, and the transcript reads that Milosevic was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- that a Kosovo Albanian woman was killed. Did you make a correction about what this soldier was actually sorry about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, he was sorry that he hadn't raped that woman first. It was a young girl. And he was very angry at this soldier who had killed her, why he didn't let him rape her first. That was the reason. I heard that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And with this correction in mind, do you attest today that the transcript from your testimony in Milosevic is true and correct and that you would give the same answers today if asked the same answers once more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the statement of April 2002 which is Exhibit P2676, then the addendum of July which is Exhibit P2679, and the transcript, Exhibit P2677. All three documents would need to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we now please call up Exhibit 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We are now calling you up a map, you will see it on your screen, and I would like to ask you some questions about the map. Sir, can you see the map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to have a look at this map when you came here last week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I had the opportunity of having a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which of the locations which are encircled on this map can you confirm as having been the locations that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: There is a place called Trnje, then Damjane, then Meca [Realtime transcript read in error "Medvedce"] --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection in respect of this way of using the map. The witness has already had various locations circled for him on this map and then he's just reading this out. I don't see what the Prosecutor wanted to achieve by doing this. I think that the witness should be shown a map without any markings and then he can make markings and locate various places on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this map was not created by the witness but by an investigator after he went in July 2002 to the different places with the witness, and I actually wanted the witness to point out one village that is circled on the map which he would not confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it makes it worse that this is a map compiled by someone else, and I don't think you should be using this map in this way. So we'll need to do it a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll leave the map for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you refer to the fact that before you were sent into Kosovo you received a so-called short-track training of two and a half months. What were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. What were you taught during these two and a half months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I was just taught how to drive, then four days of infantry training, and that was all. After two and a half months, I was sent out to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: During these two and a half months of training, did you receive any education about the laws of war, about how to behave in an armed conflict as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were you told about the Geneva Conventions or did you ever hear about them during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No. At that time I didn't hear anything about the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were you told anything about how to treat the civilian population or prisoners of war when in a combat situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after you arrived in Kosovo, did you receive any such training on the laws or on the general ways how to behave towards civilian population and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were you issued any uniforms before you were sent to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Uniform of the Army of Yugoslavia that I was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what colour was the uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, it was of a camouflage colour. One was olive-green-grey and the other one was camouflage, if I understand this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement you mention different combat groups who were operating in 1998 in the area you were deployed to as well. Would you know the name of the brigade these combat groups were part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No, the name of the brigade. Can this question be a bit clearer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me put it differently. Did you know much about the different units and brigade names in 1999 - sorry - in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, some.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So which -- which names did you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: The 82nd Paratroopers I think, if I can remember now. It was -- well, it wasn't within our barracks but it was ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But is that about what you know about brigade names or unit names or were you familiar with all the different names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, there were these special units of the police and there were these sort of SAJ people, they were called.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But coming back to the VJ, would it be fair to say that you are not, were not, and are not familiar with the names of the different brigades and units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I'm not familiar, I'm not familiar. Some -- well, I cannot really say that I find them familiar. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you were delivering rations to the different combat groups. How far away were the different combat groups away from each other, approximately, and we're talking about 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, from 20 to 30 kilometres, that was the distance from one to another, even 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how often would you do your rounds and deliver rations to the different groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Every other day -- no, every third day, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We often hear soldiers tell us which section of the army they belonged to. Now, if you're asked which grouping of the army you were part of, what's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What part of the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What unit of the army did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the logistics battalion. That is a service that provides services to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you do not know which brigade that battalion was part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm now turning to the events in Meca village in August 1998. In your statement you of it about the VJ tank firing into the village. Now, before the tank was ordered to fire, was there any firing coming from the village of Meca towards the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: There was no firing from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Was there any sign of the KLA being in that village before the tank was tired, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after the tank was discharged into the village, was then any firing coming from the village towards the VJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph of this statement are we at?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, this is page 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And it's the fourth paragraph on the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference to Meca?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's in the addendum, on the first page it refers to page 3, para 4, Meca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Meca, that's not what's being produced in the transcript. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it would be fair if the Prosecutor would put to the witness the information that she has before her, actually that he had already stated to them in this additional statement, in the addendum, that he was not sure about the village of Meca and I think that the Prosecutor knows this full well, and now she is putting leading questions to him about that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It turns out, I think, Mr. Visnjic that that's not the village in question, that we're talking about a place called Meca and that the transcript may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- I did ask -- I did mention the village of Meca because it's in the addendum, but it's not the village of Medvedce, which is far more south in the Prizren area. We're talking about a village close to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In regard to this village you also state in your statement that civilians started floating out of the house after it was shot at with the tank. Did you recognise any armed or uniformed person being among these civilians, anyone who could be said to be KLA in the broader sense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No. I just saw women and children, little children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the next village that you mention in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this is also page 3, it's the last paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And it is according to the addendum after going to this place with investigators you identified this as being the village of Rakovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that in this village there were also MUP and PJP units there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you describe what roles the different organisations had when entering a village like Rakovica. By "different organisations," I mean the VJ, the MUP, and the PJP that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I can describe the police -- well, they would get there before us and they would carry out an operation, and allegedly we would come as their support. We would carry out our tasks, whereupon we would return and they would usually stay and engage in plundering and kill whoever was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this event in the village of Rakovica in August 1998, was that actually the first time you saw VJ and police forces operating together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the first time. The first time was in Orahovac when I was there, and some of the Frenki's men were there in black uniforms with hats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Approximately before the event in Rakovica, some two weeks before that or 20, I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... If we could be directed where can we find this information where it is provided to us before in any addendum or statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Which particular information does my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reference to Frenki's men in black uniforms --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid there's no reference. I haven't heard that before myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to this part of his statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's supplementing what's there. I think you're confined, Mr. Lukic, to commenting on it in due course and you may have much to say about it to assist in our deliberations. I don't know if Ms. Moeller intends to pursue this or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I don't intend to pursue it as now any further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, you then left Kosovo in early August 1998, and on page 4 of the English version of the statement it says that you returned sometime after the OSCE mission had already been established. Can you give the month of when you approximately returned to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: October.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to turn to the events in Jeskovo around mid-March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's statement page 5, the first paragraph, Your Honours. And could we go into private session shortly, because I would like to deal with some names of his commanding officers which may reveal his identity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In your statement you referred to seven bodies that you saw, seven dead bodies that you saw, in the village. Were these male or female bodies, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: They were men. They had no military uniforms on. They wore civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No, but we found a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where did you find this hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: It was brought by a soldier. He may have taken it out of a house. I don't know whether he entered any of the houses or if he found it in the meadow. I'm not sure, but in any case he brought it with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many other weapons, if any, were found in Jeskovo, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I had no opportunity to gain any knowledge of that. It was getting dark, and we began withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move on to the events in Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Page 5 of the statement, starting with the second-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the village or close to the village, you testify in your statement that a commander - and I won't say the name now in open - ordered the company commanders to take the men into the village and kill all the civilians. Do you know which incident I refer to or would you like me to give you the name of the officer I referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I understand. It is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How do you know that this officer gave this order to the company commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I was close to them. I could overhear. I didn't hear all the details, but I heard them talking about going down to the village and to complete the operation immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you hear the particular order that you mention in your statement with your own ears issued by this officer or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How close were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Five metres, maybe 7 or 8 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, can we go back shortly into private session, please. I would like to ask him something again that may identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to the point in time when the unit returned to the barracks in Prizren. You stated that the barracks had been bombed and that the army had to move into a previously Kosovo Albanian settlement close to these barracks. How many Albanians, approximately, were forced out of the settlement in order for the VJ to move in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, the entire settlement was forced out, about 200 to 300 homes all together. They were ordered to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And around which time did this approximately happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: It happened on the fifth day of the bombing, when we returned from the village of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And from there onwards, how long did you, you and your units, stay in this settlement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: During these two and a half months, did you observe any -- ever any groups of people passing by the settlement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Through the settlement, no one. No one dared to. Every day I watched refugees going to Albania on foot or on tractors. Tractors were full of refugees, the tractor-trailers were full.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that you watched while you were at the settlement close to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate of how many people you think you saw passing by during these two and a half months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, the first seven or eight days I didn't see anyone. After that, every day refugees were passing down that road every day or practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which direction were they going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: From the direction of Suva Reka towards Albania and also from the direction of Djakovica towards Albania, or rather, the border crossing. I can't remember. I can't remember the name of the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And your unit and the soldiers who saw these refugees passing by, did you do anything in regard to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: On page 7 of the statement the second paragraph, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You referred to your involvement in the stealing of cars and trucks. How did you get involved in this? Can you tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, it just so happened that I managed to ignite a car. There was no key. I hot-wired it and nobody else knew how to do it except for me, and word spread throughout the unit and then my commander and his NCOs and officers would always bring me to a car to turn it on my hot-wiring it and to bring it in for it to be used for army purposes, for army purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we shortly go into private session. I would like to know the names of these officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: One second before you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How many other soldiers like you were involved in getting these cars and trucks for the use of the army, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a lot of them, but I cannot give you the exact number. They were in other units and I didn't really know them that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many cars and trucks did you personally take this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: You want me to tell you exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, I took about four small cars, four trucks, and three combi-vans.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what do you mean when you say in your statement that good cars were taken? What was considered a good car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, those cars -- well, how can I say? For us in the army, all of them were good, the ones we took.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what happened to these cars when the army withdrew from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I know about two for sure, that they were not taken up there to Serbia. As for the others, I wasn't down there at the time because I was allowed to go home six days before the withdrawal. And when I came back to finish my military service in the town where I was asked to come, then I noticed up there some of the vehicles that I had taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you said you noticed them. Were you positive that these were the exact cars that you had actually taken in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I'm sure that those were the ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo in 1999, did you see any other looting or stealing taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw things being taken out of Albanian houses, things that are things that one has in a house like TVs and TV antennas, and things like that. I know that a policeman barged into a house together with us, that is to say with the army. And I remember when he took some money from a box.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where was that, which village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: This settlement where we had expelled the Albanians, and then we settled down there. The settlement right below the barracks, the settlement where we had expelled the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That would be the one close to Prizren. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Prizren, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who -- you said you saw things being taken out. Who took these things, apart from the one occasion where you mentioned the policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, for example, some officers were taken -- taking things out, and their troops were helping them carry these things out. A friend of mine, as a matter of fact, told me that before the withdrawal they were loading trucks. For example, they'd load a truck from a house, they'd fill up the truck, because Albanians had good things in their houses as a rule, so they would take all of their things, these officers would take all of their things, and take them to Serbia for their own use.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know the names of some of these officers? And just say yes or no at this point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I don't know the names, but anyway, every officer has rank insignia so I knew that they were officers. A soldier couldn't have ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your addendum you referred to another incident involving the killing of three Albanian men, and you referred to your commander giving two of the men who were shot a cigarette and then shooting them. I would like to give us -- I would like you to give us the name of this officer, but again I would like to go into private session first, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back -- we are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I inquire from Your Honours when you intend to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I have three more questions or so, so I should be able to finish by then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, in your transcript you referred to a border crossing called Vrmice. I hope I pronounce it understandably, and you said in your previous testimony that at this border crossing policemen were taking documents from Albanians and set them on fire. Did you see this with your own eyes? Were you at this border crossing at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No, I didn't see this with my own eyes, but they told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, I had this soldier there who came from the same place that I came from and he's the one who told me about this. Quite simply, I saw him and he told me about this, what it was that was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Also in your transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, the reference for this -- for the documents and border crossing is page 8253 in the transcript. And I now move on to page 8251.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where you, sir, referred to the fact that you drove the deputy of your unit commander to certain meetings. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you testified that from the stories this deputy told you, you concluded that there was a plan to expel the Albanians from Kosovo. Can you give us some more details of the stories this deputy told you what -- which made you think that there was a plan of Kosovo Albanians being expelled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, there's not much I can really say about this. I know that once I was told they should all be thrown out. I talked to him a bit and I sort of said, pretending, "Yes, yes, right," just for the hell of it. And he said, "Well, that's what we are working for, that's what we're working for." "That's what we're working for" means this plan of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know the name of this deputy? And just say yes or no at this stage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session one more time, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, you left Kosovo, you said, a week -- sorry, around the 6th of June, 1999. And in your statement, page 7, you say that you took a bus from Pristina to Mitrovica. How was the situation in Pristina at that time? What did you see when you came to Pristina to board the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, the situation was very bad. I saw policemen from the special unit shooting in a particular direction, and the neighbourhood behind that policeman were all on fire, all the houses. I ran quickly from one bus to another, so that's the only thing I could see and shooting could be heard, the real thing, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. Which city did you now talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I'm talking about the place around the bus station in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I thought there was a misunderstanding, because I had asked you about Pristina first. Did you observe anything particular in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: In Pristina, I didn't observe anything and as for the area around Pristina, between Pristina and Mitrovica, villages were on fire. There was smoke there and tank fire could be heard. It could be heard pretty well from the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So just to clarify what you just described. You watched while you were on the bus between Pristina and Mitrovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that completes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. Zecevic, what order are we likely to have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to follow the indictment order in this case, and Mr. Milutinovic's Defence doesn't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is some mistake. I'll be last, so Mr. Lazarevic will be before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when we return we can pick up with the cross-examination. We'll go into closed session for the witness to leave the court. We have to have a break at this stage, sir, so in a moment you will leave the courtroom with the usher and he will bring you back once the break is over.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I want to talk to you primarily, and perhaps exclusively, about only one of the operations that you've talked about in your Milosevic testimony and your statement and your testimony here today, and that is the operation in mid-March 1999 at Jeskovo. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Milosevic -- your testimony in Milosevic at page 8233 you talk about being very near to General Delic on the morning when you approached that village. You said you were only 20 to 30 metres away from him; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you claim that you heard him say that, "We should not let a single person remain alive"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you say that you heard him on the radio describe that when a shell was fired on the village, that would be basically the signal for the battle to begin. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm having trouble relating those two incidents. In the one place you're 20 or 30 metres away from him and you hear him say what you claim he said; and then in the other time you're hearing by radio. How much -- how far apart are those in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: When I was some 20 to 30 metres away, it was one and a half hours after the occasion on which he had ordered the tank to fire a shell, when we went down to the village. We all got close and went from one house to the next. That's when I heard him say, "Kill everyone you come across."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did, and that's the answer I was looking for. So once the tank shell exploded in the village, you claim that you then began an attack and fired on the village for about a half an hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, around half an hour or 20 minutes. Then we stopped and waited. Supposedly, we were waiting to see whether there would be any new developments down there in the village. Since nothing was happening, we were told to develop into a skirmish line and go down towards the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. What I'm trying to do is finish my cross of you rather quickly, so I would hope that if I ask you a question that can be easily answered that you do that and if I want an explanation I'll ask you for it. Were you firing an automatic weapon in that first half-hour when you fired on the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I did not for sure; others did, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did not for sure what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Fire in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you did no firing at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I did not fire at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Milosevic you were asked by Mr. Ryneveld regarding this: "After the tank shell had been fired at the village," page 8234, Mr. Ryneveld asked you: "What happened next?" And you said: "We were shooting for about half an hour I think, all of us." Now, doesn't "all of us" include you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I was speaking in general terms about the army, we, the army. I did not open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So anybody who would read your statement: "We were shooting for about half an hour, all of us," would be foolish to think that included you. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that firing that was not done by you lasted for about half an hour and then stopped for about an hour, and then that's when you say General Delic then ordered that you form a skirmish line and approach the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think it's your testimony that you saw one person killed -- actually observed one person being killed and that you saw seven dead bodies at that scene, and according to you, everyone that you saw there that had been killed was dressed in civilian clothes; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you later heard after you had returned to barracks from apparently your fellow soldiers that 30 persons had been killed there who you believe were all civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, and I saw that these people were civilians. They had no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that Commander Delic testified in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't know that he testified in that case after you had testified and that he was asked about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I will tell you that at page 41772 General Delic claims that in your respective testimonies in Milosevic, you and Witness K41 were trying to cover each other for crimes the two of you committed later on. He says you came to testify because you had committed a crime and that you took refuge from the police in the house of K41. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: It is a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you and K41 ever accused of committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No. He was. I was not. As for him being accused, I don't know where the real problem lay. Currently he's serving a prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, you were never sought by the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that period of time after you had returned from Kosovo, did you have a passport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What happened to your passport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I had my passport made after I have served -- after I had served my military term. Had I had a passport before that, they would never have seen my face in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General Delic also says at page 41773 that on this day you're talking about at Jeskovo your unit, the logistics unit, never entered Jeskovo. He says you were a logistics person and you only went to Hoca Zagradska, which is I think about 3 kilometres from the scene. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: It is incorrect that we were not there. I think we were the most numerous in that barracks, although we were a logistics battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things that's a bit difficult to understand about your testimony is that part of the time you're involved in logistics and you're driving a truck and you're delivering supplies to various combat units, and then you claim part of the time you are a combat unit and you're involved in all these combat activities which General Delic says couldn't happen because you had logistics responsibilities when these actions were going on to supply the troops that were involved in the combat. And then you also claim that you spent time driving someone back and forth to meetings. It seems that you were an awfully busy person. Is that all true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: What you said is incorrect. Do you want me to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that would be good if you explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Before I deserted from the army, I spent two and a half members as a -- two and a half months as a member of the Combat Group 2 in Damjane. I spent over two months there and I knew things sufficiently well. Second of all, when I was returned by the army to the same unit, I was not made part of any combat groups, but I supplied food and water. Therefore, every third day I brought supplies to all combat groups. I can explain further if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's good enough. I need to tell you so you can have a chance to comment about it that General Delic told the Judges in the Milosevic case at 41777 that basically everything you were saying was complete nonsense, that you couldn't possibly have seen or observed any of the things you claim to have observed, partly because you weren't there, partly because they did not happen. And one of the things that General Delic referred to was a report, a writing, it's a little vague, but apparently from an Albanian -- Kosovo Albanian writer about a KLA commander, and this is 41779, who spoke in the book about the KLA heroes who were killed there at Jeskovo that day and listed their names of those people. He said: "They are soldiers belonging to the special unit of the 125th Brigade of the operative zone of Pastrik. It was a great loss indeed because the fighting was head to head at a distance of 15 to 20 metres." Now, I take it that you deny that that KLA officer is telling the truth about what happened there at Jeskovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the OSCE, Organisation For Security and Cooperation in Europe, as part of the Kosovo Verification Mission, made a report about what had happened there in Jeskovo that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the electronic data system was not available to me over the weekend for reasons I still don't understand. So what I have is a couple of pages from ""As Seen, As Told"" but apparently it's going into the system -- it's been found and will go into the system by the Lazarevic group today, the actual report, but what I have is an account from that from "As Seen, As Told."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, here is -- this was also presented to the Milosevic Chamber by General Delic. Here's what OSCE said about Jeskovo. "On 11 March the security forces conducted a joint operation against the UCK in Jeskovo south-west of Prizren. The VJ deployed in Hoca Zagradska, Bilusa, and Bijac. Approximately eight tanks with armoured personnel carriers, artillery, and mortars were used by the VJ. The OSCE/KVM verifiers observed," indicating they were there and watching, "a heavy bombardment of Jeskovo and reported buildings burning. The UCK was reported to have responded by mounting an attack in the area of Zociste using mortars and heavy machine-guns. The OSCE/KVM Prizren regional centre commented that the UCK had infiltrated into Jeskovo, a previously deserted village." Now, the OSCE is indicating that that village was deserted except for KLA that had moved in there, UCK that had moved in there, and yet you're telling us that people killed there were civilians. You're just not telling the truth, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: How can a village be deserted if there was another village 2 to 3 kilometres away which was full and there we took all the people out of the houses and we searched the houses for terrorists, and then there was the next village. We went through all those villages; therefore, how could the first one have been empty? I cannot understand. Before Jeskovo, there were two villages from which we took all of the villagers out of and we searched all their -- all of their houses in those two villages. As for Jeskovo to be deserted, well, in such a context I fail to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't answer my question. The OSCE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question, Mr. Ackerman, is not one to which you're likely to get an answer that's going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to my question as: "You're just not telling the truth, are you?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the one, yes. It's so often viewed by witnesses here as an assertion rather than a question and you inevitably find that the answer is tangential to the question, and even if he had answered the question where would it have taken us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he could have said: You're correct, I'm not telling the truth," and that would have taken us quite a way, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that testimony in Milosevic by General Delic, he was asked by Judge Robinson why he thought you would come there and tell a pack of lies. And what he said was, and I quote him -- actually, he testified precisely to confirm the allegations made by Witness K41, who protected him at the time from police prosecution due to the crime he committed. "He was probably given a promise that if he testified he would perhaps be removed from the country and that he would get away from the arm of justice." Now, one of the things that General Delic said in that answer was you were probably given a promise of relocation so as to avoid the arm of justice. What I want to know is: Have you been promised relocation? Have you been given relocation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Who was to promise us anything? No one promised us anything. I and K41 live 250 kilometres apart. We have no contact. After the army we went home together, but the only contact or the initial contact we had was when I asked him to come and testify. As for the stories of us being criminals, well, that is simply incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. My question was: Did you -- have you been relocated or have you been promised that you would be relocated?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness answered this question. He said: "No one promised us anything."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I heard, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That may be part of the question, Your Honour. The other part was: Has he been relocated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you deal with that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we have not been relocated. I never asked for any relocations and he didn't either. Are you happy with the answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm really happy with that answer and I'm just about to tell you why. You gave a statement on the 20th of June, 2003, to interviewer Barney Kelly, and page 28 of that statement you said --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, just a moment, please. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If we are going into the circumstances, the personal circumstances of this witness, I would want to have this in private session, because you know the background of the witness and I think there is a danger that his identity may be disclosed otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am aware of that, and I'll go into private session when we need to. We don't need to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before I was interrupted I was telling you that I was very happy you gave me that answer, because you'd been interviewed by Barney Kelly on the 20th of June, 2003, where in paragraph 28 you told him: "I will agree to testify in The Hague if I am relocated." You just told us you'd never asked for relocation. That wasn't the truth, was it? You told the Judges an untruth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No. I'll explain. He asked me whether -- or rather, I asked him if I could go on to a third country to be relocated if my identity became known, and he said, "Well, it's up to you to decide, but I'm not sure you will be given a relocation to another state since we have no such programmes in place." That's what he explained to me; however, I did -- I did ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, a little while ago you told us you didn't ask for that and now you're telling us you did. And I was quoting from a statement that has your signature on every page, and I'd be very happy to show it to you if you'd want to see it. If you deny your signature is on every page, I'm going to insist you look at it. Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly how things went that day when I gave the statement. I can't recall him making any promises as for the relocation. However, I deny your claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
