utterances.text: Where's the disagreement here, Mr. Ackerman? The witness is saying he did ask for relocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The disagreement, Your Honour, is right before I asked him about that statement, he told you he didn't ask for relocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But why is it you're now emphasising he signed every page of the statement when he agrees with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's waffled about it. I'd like to find it before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you're putting to him from the statement: "I will agree to testify in The Hague if I'm relocated." And in answer to your later question he said that: "Yes, I did ask for that." We don't seem to be disagreeing about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He says that came as a result of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand he made an explanation for that, but you won't get an answer to that in the statement that he has signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, all right. I'm finished. I think now is a time when we probably do need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked about testifying and about being relocated. Did I understand you correctly in terms of the previous testimony you gave and the statement that you gave, that you have relatives who are Albanians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I do not have any Albanian relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 8290 in your previous testimony, when you say that everybody were -- was shouting at you, "You fool, don't go to Kosovo. You see that there is a war going on there. That's what most people said, and I agreed. I decided not to go back and I have quite a few Albanian relatives."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I live in a place where there are Albanians. Do you understand that? Secondly, if I as a Bosniak go there, I mean, since we have the same faith. If I went to wage war against Albanians, they thought that I was doing it on purpose, you see. That's why I said that. If I go to Kosovo, the Albanians are going to treat me -- well, they're not going to like me. Do you understand me? Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we understand each other, and my next question was and you said now that your own setting is primarily Muslim and Albanian. Without referring to the actual place that you live in, can you tell me what the percentage of the Albanian and the Muslim population is and what percentage of the population is Orthodox?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: This is the way it is: 70 per cent are Bosniaks, 10 per cent are Serbs, and the rest are Albanians. That's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it correct then, Mr. K54, that you are not afraid of the 10 per cent of the Serbs that are there, if we take into account your testimony, but that you are afraid of the 90 per cent of Albanians and Muslims if you do not testify in accordance with their will. Isn't that more correct than what you said previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: You listen to me. I'm not afraid of my own people. I'm afraid only of those people who are not my own and this time I went -- well,, allegedly, to speak against those 10 per cent. That's the way they see it. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're in fear of this 10 per cent, that they are going to find out about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you one thing, those 10 per cent are like 100 per cent down there. They do any kind of thing. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we do. However, you will have to pause between my question and your answer because we speak the same language. You said just now that the captain who we mentioned - we are not going to mention his name now because we are not in private session - you said that he liked you to drive him because you were the oldest driver. What does that mean in terms of age or experience or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Age and experience. He was full of fear as far as driving was concerned. He liked to be driven by somebody who knew how to drive well, and he established that I was the one. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: well, you know, he took me everywhere with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "in terms of experience," how long was your experience as a driver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I have been driving since 1994 -- actually, I got my licence that year, but I started driving two or three years before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your experience goes as far back as 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How did you complete a fast-track course in Kraljevo, which lasted two and a half months, as you mention in your statement on paragraph 2, paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I am surprised by that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't understand. You had your driver's licence since 1994, but then you decided to attend a driver's course and it lasted for two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: It was a surprise for me to have to undergo such training because I knew all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you said to the officers that you know how to drive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: And based on the driver's licence they can see the category of vehicle I was permitted to drive. They were probably not that stupid so as to fail to see which categories of vehicles I could operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Therefore, you underwent a fast-track training because, as you said, you have been driving since 1994 and the complete training would otherwise have taken six months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes, it lasted for only two and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's because you had been driving since 1994. Had you been unable to drive, then what would have been the length of training, a year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that in all training centres of the VJ, according to the programme, the training takes two months and 22 days for each soldier. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I did not. I know that I was familiar with the term of six months. I knew of that. I knew that one had to undergo six months of training because no training can be completed in two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that your conclusion and your line of thinking, or did you hear that from someone specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I heard that from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: When I was in the army, the training is usually six months, but they told us "We will shorten it because of the situation," and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: The officers in Kraljevo who taught us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I've forgotten their names. I can try to recall them, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very well. Further in your statement, in the following paragraph you say, as you confirmed today during your examination-in-chief, that you arrived at Prizren on the 10th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spent a fortnight at the VJ headquarters in the northern outskirts of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was that headquarters as a soldier that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: It was a barracks of Car Dusan Silni. I was a member of the rear battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it a headquarters or a barracks? You said you spent a fortnight there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Headquarters, barracks. For me it's a staff, a headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A headquarters of what brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: Ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was your brigade? You spent over a year in that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I can't remember. I really cannot recall. I even forgot the military post where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it seems that you remember quite a lot of detail about other things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54
utterances.text: I remember the bad things. The good things did not stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this may be a proper moment to break for the day. I see that it's quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. We need to go into closed session for the witness to leave the courtroom. We need to finish our session for today at this stage, but you are required to return tomorrow to continue and complete your evidence; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile - and this is very important, apart from the fact that some of the blinds aren't working - it's very important that you do not discuss any part of your evidence with anybody; that's either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give. You can talk to whoever you like about whatever you like except the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
